questions.prompt: Over a 60 s run with ground truth, the mean NEES of a 3-dof pose filter is 9. What does this mean?
options: The filter is overconfident: its covariance is about three times smaller than the real errors justify.
The filter is very accurate, because a large NEES means the estimate is close to the truth in absolute metres.
The filter is underconfident, because a large NEES means the reported covariance is far too large for the errors.
Nothing can be concluded, because NEES values are only meaningful for a filter without a gyro bias state.
questions.explanation: NEES is the squared error normalised by the covariance; its expectation is the dimension (3). A mean of 9 means errors are larger than P admits.

questions.prompt: A simulated camera is 480 pixels high with a vertical field of view of 45 degrees. What is the ideal focal length in pixels?
The bearing is predicted as -3.10 rad and measured as +3.10 rad. Which innovation should the EKF use?
options: +6.20 rad, because the update must use the exact difference of the two numbers without any modification.
About -0.083 rad: the raw difference 6.20 rad wrapped into [-pi, pi).
0 rad, because the two angles describe the same direction and therefore the update can be skipped.
+3.10 rad, because the innovation is limited to the measured bearing when the sign differs.
questions.explanation: Angles are circular; an unwrapped 6.2 rad innovation would throw the pose far off.

questions.prompt: Why do we update the covariance in Joseph form, P = (I-KH)P(I-KH)^T + K R K^T?
options: It makes the filter converge faster than the standard form, because it uses a larger effective gain.
It removes the need for the gate, because the extra term already rejects measurement outliers on its own.
It is a sum of positive semi-definite terms, so P stays symmetric and positive definite even with rounding or a non-optimal gain.
It avoids computing the matrix inverse of S, which cannot be done on a laptop in less than a millisecond.
questions.explanation: The standard update (I-KH)P is only equivalent for the exact optimal gain and loses symmetry in floating point.

questions.prompt: A gate at the 99 % chi-square quantile (2 dof) is applied to 770 good detections. About how many are expected to be rejected?
No marker is visible for 20 s. What should the reported covariance do, and why?
options: It should stay constant, because the last correction fixed the pose and the gyro keeps it exact while the wheel odometry adds nothing.
It should shrink, because every prediction step adds information about the pose from the wheel odometry.
It should be reset to its initial value, because the filter has lost track and must start again from scratch.
It should grow, because the pose is only predicted and nothing bounds the accumulated odometry and gyro errors.
questions.explanation: Prediction adds process noise; only a landmark measurement reduces uncertainty.

questions.prompt: You tuned Q and R on trajectories 1000 to 1004 and report the accuracy on the same five. What is the flaw?
options: The numbers measure how well you fitted those runs; tune on other seeds, freeze, then test once on 1000 to 1004.
There is no flaw as long as the thresholds are met, because the seeds are fixed and the runs are reproducible.
The flaw is that five trajectories are too few, so the only fix is to add more trajectories to the same tuning set.
The flaw is that Q and R should never be tuned; they must be copied from the sensor datasheets without change.
questions.explanation: Reusing data for tuning and test hides overfitting.

questions.prompt: A run has mean NEES 9.0 but mean NIS 2.0. Name the most likely cause and the first thing you would change.
rubric: Identifies an overconfident prediction step: process noise Q too small or a missing state such as the gyro bias.
Notes that NIS near 2 says the measurement noise R and the landmark model are about right, so R is not the first suspect.
Proposes increasing Q (or adding the bias state), then re-running on separate tuning seeds and checking NEES again.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
